body:
Industrial effluent is different from municipal sewage

Industrial effluent is wastewater produced by manufacturing or other industrial activities. Its composition depends on the process. Textile-processing effluent, for example, may contain dyes and other processing chemicals, while chemical industries can generate wastewater containing substances that require specialised treatment.

Municipal sewage mainly originates from households and other urban activities. Although municipal sewage can also contain harmful contaminants, its treatment needs generally differ from those of many industrial effluents.

Industrial wastewater therefore cannot automatically be treated, reused or discharged in the same manner as domestic sewage.

Important treatment systems

SystemPurposeImportant distinction
STP: Sewage Treatment PlantTreats municipal or domestic sewageTreatment does not necessarily mean the water is reused
ETP: Effluent Treatment PlantTreats industrial wastewaterUsually designed for the characteristics of specified industrial effluent
CETP: Common Effluent Treatment PlantProvides shared treatment for effluent received from multiple industrial unitsParticipating units may still need pretreatment and individual compliance
Tertiary treatmentImproves treated-water quality for specified requirementsNot every tertiary-treated stream is suitable for every use
ZLD: Zero Liquid DischargeSeeks to prevent liquid effluent discharge from the systemResidual salts, sludge and other wastes still require management

How a common effluent treatment plant works

A Common Effluent Treatment Plant (CETP) receives compatible wastewater from several industrial units and treats it at a shared facility. This arrangement can reduce the need for every enterprise to operate a complete separate treatment system.

Shared treatment is particularly useful in industrial estates containing small and medium enterprises. However, different units may generate very different effluent qualities. Where required, a unit must carry out suitable pretreatment before sending wastewater to the common plant.

Treatment can produce water suitable for permitted discharge or, after any necessary additional treatment, for reuse. It can also produce sludge or other residues that require appropriate handling. Whether a particular residue is hazardous depends on its characteristics and applicable rules.

Examples of shared treatment infrastructure in Gujarat

GIDC's published infrastructure information identifies common effluent treatment facilities associated with several Gujarat industrial areas, including Ankleshwar and Panoli, Nandesari, Sachin and Pandesara, Vapi and Sarigam, and the Naroda, Vatva and Odhav areas of Ahmedabad.

These examples illustrate the importance of shared environmental infrastructure in industrial clusters. The existence of a CETP should not be interpreted as proof that all connected units comply with their obligations or that the treated effluent is entirely reused.

Understanding zero liquid discharge

Zero Liquid Discharge (ZLD) is an approach intended to prevent the release of liquid wastewater from a particular treatment system. Water may be recovered for reuse, while concentrated residues remain for further management.

ZLD is different from ordinary effluent treatment followed by permitted discharge. It is also different from waste prevention: a ZLD facility may consume energy and produce residual solids or concentrated waste.

Zero liquid discharge does not mean zero pollution or zero solid waste. Any recovered water, remaining salts, sludge and other residues must be managed safely. Environmental assessment must consider the entire process, not only the absence of a liquid outlet.

Why prevention remains important

Reducing wastewater generation at the production stage can make subsequent treatment easier and less resource-intensive. For example, better water management in a manufacturing process may reduce the volume of wastewater requiring treatment. Preventing contamination is generally preferable to allowing unnecessary pollution and attempting to remove it later.

Prelims focus

  • STP is associated primarily with municipal or domestic sewage.
  • ETP is associated with industrial effluent.
  • CETP means Common Effluent Treatment Plant and serves multiple industrial units.
  • Gujarat examples include treatment facilities associated with Ankleshwar–Panoli, Nandesari, Sachin–Pandesara and Vapi–Sarigam.
  • ZLD concerns liquid discharge, not the complete elimination of all waste.
  • Trap: Effluent treatment, compliant discharge and wastewater reuse are 3 distinct outcomes.

[Sources: NCERT, Class 12, India: People and Economy, chapter 6, Water Resources, sections Deterioration of Water Quality, Prevention of Water Pollution and Recycle and Reuse of Water, printed pp. 65–67; Gujarat Industrial Development Corporation, Details of Various Infrastructure Services and Facilities in GIDC, Effluent Treatment Plant table, published document consulted 2 November 2026; Gujarat Industrial Development Corporation, Useful Links, Vapi Waste and Effluent Management facility information, consulted 2 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Industrial units pretreat effluent where required before shared CETP treatment, which produces water for discharge or suitable reuse and residues for management.
pictures.caption: A CETP provides shared treatment, while individual factories retain responsibility for their effluents.

title: Industrial Effluent Treatment, Common Facilities and Zero Liquid Discharge

body:
Waste can contain recoverable resources

Industrial and urban activities produce several types of solid waste. Some materials can be reused directly, some can be recycled into useful inputs, and some require specialised treatment or final disposal.

Material recovery means collecting and separating usable materials from discarded products or waste streams. Recycling involves processing suitable waste into materials that can be used again.

For example, segregated metal scrap can be processed for further metal production. Appropriate plastic waste may be sorted and recycled, although the suitability of different plastics depends on composition, contamination and available recycling arrangements.

Different routes for managing waste

Waste-management routeMain purposeExample
ReuseUse a suitable product or component againReusing serviceable equipment or containers
Material recyclingRecover usable materialReprocessing segregated metal scrap
Biological processingRecover value from biodegradable wasteComposting suitable organic waste
Energy recoveryObtain useful energy from suitable wasteUsing an appropriate combustible residual fraction as fuel
Safe disposalControl risks from unusable residuesDisposing of specified residues at an authorised facility

What is co-processing?

Co-processing is the use of suitable waste in an industrial process to replace part of the conventional fuel, raw material or both. Cement manufacturing provides an important example because cement kilns require substantial heat and mineral inputs.

Some appropriately selected residual wastes can supply useful heat in a cement kiln. Other suitable wastes may contribute mineral constituents to the cement-making process. This is why co-processing can provide both energy recovery and material substitution.

The waste must be suitable for the process. Its composition, contamination, environmental effects and applicable permissions are important. Co-processing is not a general licence to burn any unwanted material.

Refuse-derived fuel and cement kilns

Refuse-derived fuel (RDF) is a fuel prepared from suitable combustible waste fractions. For municipal solid waste, the relevant material is generally the non-recyclable combustible fraction remaining after suitable segregation and processing.

Under the Solid Waste Management Rules, 2026, the definition of combustible waste includes non-biodegradable, non-recyclable, non-reusable and non-hazardous solid waste with a calorific value exceeding 1500 kcal/kg, excluding chlorinated materials. The rules define municipal-waste co-processing in terms of the relevant suitable non-biodegradable, non-recyclable solid-waste fraction.

This definition should not be confused with the separate framework governing co-processing of hazardous and other industrial wastes. Such wastes are subject to the Hazardous and Other Wastes (Management and Transboundary Movement) Rules, 2016, as amended, and relevant Central Pollution Control Board guidelines.

Why segregation must come first

Consider a mixed waste stream containing paper, metal, food residues, plastic packaging and unsuitable contaminated material. Sending the entire mixture directly for thermal treatment would ignore the possibility of recycling useful materials and may introduce unsuitable substances into the process.

A resource-efficient system instead separates the fractions that can be safely reused or recycled, processes suitable organic waste and assesses whether the remaining combustible fraction can be recovered under applicable conditions.

Separate waste rules continue to govern materials such as hazardous industrial waste, electronic waste, batteries and biomedical waste. These categories should not be mixed indiscriminately into municipal waste or ordinary RDF.

Environmental safeguards and limitations

Co-processing must comply with applicable authorisation and emission requirements. For hazardous and other wastes, authorisation must be obtained from the relevant state pollution control board before utilisation, on the basis of applicable CPCB standard operating procedures or guidelines.

Although appropriately managed co-processing may reduce demand for conventional fuels and mineral resources, it does not remove the need to control emissions or manage unsuitable residues. A waste stream that can be recycled safely into a useful material should not automatically be diverted to energy recovery merely because it is combustible.

Recycling recovers usable material.
Energy recovery obtains useful energy.
Co-processing uses suitable waste as an industrial fuel, raw material or both.
Disposal manages remaining waste that cannot be appropriately recovered.

Prelims focus

  • Co-processing can replace part of the conventional fuel or raw-material requirement of an industrial process.
  • Cement kilns are an important example of co-processing.
  • RDF stands for Refuse-Derived Fuel.
  • The Solid Waste Management Rules, 2026, specify a calorific value exceeding 1500 kcal/kg in their definition of suitable combustible municipal solid waste.
  • Hazardous-waste co-processing is governed by its separate regulatory framework.
  • Trap: Co-processing is not identical to material recycling, and not all waste is suitable for co-processing.

[Sources: Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change, Solid Waste Management Rules, 2026, notification S.O. 388(E), dated 27 January 2026, rules 3 and 5, including definitions of combustible waste, co-processing and waste hierarchy; Central Pollution Control Board, Guidelines for Pre-processing and Co-processing of Hazardous and Other Wastes in Cement Plant as per the Hazardous and Other Wastes Rules, 2016, sections 2–7, annexed to CPCB's submission in National Green Tribunal Original Application 112 of 2023; Hazardous and Other Wastes (Management and Transboundary Movement) Rules, 2016, rule 9. Sources consulted 2 November 2026.]

title: Material Recovery, Waste Recycling and Cement-Kiln Co-processing

body:
Why ports are relevant to the circular economy

Gujarat's coastline supports ports, maritime transport, coastal industries and ship recycling. Ports connect industrial production with domestic and international trade, while also handling materials, equipment, packaging, fuels and different waste streams.

Resource-efficient port operations can reduce avoidable material losses, encourage appropriate reuse and recycling, improve water management and prevent waste from reaching coastal waters.

However, ports are not automatically circular-economy facilities. Their contribution depends on the actual systems used for collecting, treating, recovering and safely managing materials.

Important coastal locations in Gujarat

LocationGeographical and economic connection
Deendayal Port, formerly KandlaMajor port in Kutch, connected with the Gulf of Kutch
MundraCommercial port in Kutch
DahejPort and industrial area associated with Bharuch district
HaziraPort and industrial area associated with Surat
Alang–SosiyaShip recycling yard in the Bhavnagar coastal region

These locations should not be treated as identical facilities. Deendayal Port is a major port administered through its own port authority. Gujarat Maritime Board has responsibilities relating to the state's non-major port sector and associated maritime infrastructure, including the Alang ship recycling yard.

Alang–Sosiya ship recycling yard

Alang–Sosiya, near Bhavnagar, is an important ship recycling location. According to the Gujarat Maritime Board, the yard began operations in 1982–83.

When a ship reaches the end of its useful service life, it may still contain substantial quantities of recoverable materials. These include steel and potentially reusable machinery, fittings and other components.

Recovering suitable steel scrap allows that material to return to productive use rather than requiring equivalent quantities of newly obtained raw material. Reusable components may also retain value when they are safe and suitable for further use.

Ship recycling also produces hazardous waste

An old ship is not simply a collection of useful metal. It can contain oil residues, contaminated materials, insulation and other substances that require special handling. Certain insulation materials and coatings may contain hazardous substances.

Therefore, resource recovery must be accompanied by measures to protect workers, coastal land and nearby waters. Unsafe dismantling can transfer pollution from an old ship into the surrounding environment.

The Gujarat Maritime Board describes a Treatment, Storage and Disposal Facility (TSDF) associated with environmental management at Alang. Its described facilities include an effluent treatment plant, an incinerator and landfill cells.

A TSDF is intended for the controlled treatment, storage or disposal of specified wastes. It is not the same as an ordinary municipal waste collection centre.

Other circular-economy opportunities at ports

Port-related resource efficiency can include preventing cargo and packaging losses, segregating reusable materials, recovering appropriate scrap and supplying treated water for suitable non-potable purposes.

Ship-generated waste, oily residues and other controlled materials require management under the rules applicable to them. Coastal conditions make pollution prevention especially important because waste entering the marine environment can damage aquatic ecosystems and affect coastal livelihoods.

Recovering scrap is only one part of responsible ship recycling. The recovery of valuable steel does not justify uncontrolled release of oil, hazardous substances or contaminated wastewater.

Prelims focus

  • Deendayal Port is the present name of Kandla Port, located in Kutch.
  • Dahej is associated with Bharuch, while Hazira is associated with Surat.
  • Alang–Sosiya is associated with ship recycling in the Bhavnagar region.
  • Gujarat Maritime Board records the beginning of Alang–Sosiya ship recycling operations in 1982–83.
  • TSDF stands for Treatment, Storage and Disposal Facility.
  • Trap: Gujarat Maritime Board and Deendayal Port Authority should not be treated as the same institution.

[Sources: Gujarat Maritime Board, Ship Recycling Yards, Alang–Sosiya section, and Environment FAQs, questions on Alang environmental management and port environmental responsibilities, consulted 2 November 2026; Gujarat Maritime Board, State of Art Disposal of Hazardous Waste Environment Management Infrastructure at Alang, Treatment, Storage and Disposal Facility section; Deendayal Port Authority, port location and site information; Gujarat Maritime Board, Dahej Port and Last Mile Connectivity sections, consulted 2 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Alang–Sosiya demonstrates the resource-recovery opportunities and environmental risks associated with ship recycling.
